Torre Pellice
tor'reh pel'lee-cheh
n. (chief town of the Waldensian valleys in Piedmont; seat of the Waldensian synod)
From Italian torre, a tower, and the river Pellice; the valley name in Piedmontese Val Pelis.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Torre Pellice is the principal town of the Val Pellice and the administrative centre of the Waldensian church. The Waldenses had held the three valleys of Pellice, Chisone and Germanasca since the thirteenth century, dissenting from Rome before the Reformation existed, and they survived there through crusade, inquisition, massacre and exile until the Letters Patent of 1848 gave them civil rights; the synod and the Table, their governing body, have met in Torre Pellice since, with a college, a library and a hospital in the town. The dictionary records it because the Waldensian valleys are the plainest European instance of a doctrine Scripture states repeatedly and the church forgets in every prosperous generation: that God preserves a remnant, and that the remnant is small, and that its survival is not its own achievement. “Even so then at this present time also there is a remnant according to the election of grace” (Rom 11:5).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a remnant as that which is left, a residue; election as the choice of God in selecting a person or persons to his favour; and a valley as a hollow or low tract of land between hills.

expand to see more

REMNANT, n. [from remain.] That which is left after the separation, removal or destruction of a part; residue.

ELECTION, n. [L. electio.] The choice of God, by which persons are distinguished as objects of mercy; divine choice.

VALLEY, n. [L. vallis.] A hollow or low tract of land between hills or mountains.

SYNOD, n. [Gr. an assembly.] A council or meeting of ecclesiastics to consult on matters of religion.

Key Scripture

Rom 11:5 — "Even so then at this present time also there is a remnant according to the election of grace."

Isa 1:9 — "Except the LORD of hosts had left unto us a very small remnant, we should have been as Sodom, and we should have been like unto Gomorrah."

Rom 9:27 — "Esaias also crieth concerning Israel, Though the number of the children of Israel be as the sand of the sea, a remnant shall be saved:"

Rev 12:6 — "And the woman fled into the wilderness, where she hath a place prepared of God, that they should feed her there a thousand two hundred and threescore days."

Modern Corruption

The Waldensian capital in the Val Pellice; the synod and Table have met here since the civil rights of 1848.

expand to see more

The corruption to name is Rome's treatment of the Waldenses as heretics to be exterminated, which was pursued by crusade in 1487, by the Inquisition for three centuries, and by massacre as late as 1655 and 1686. The dictionary names it plainly and does not accept the modern framing in which this becomes a regrettable misunderstanding on both sides. A second and gentler corruption threatens the valleys now: a church that survived by doctrine being commended chiefly for its tolerance and its tourism.

The principle to recover is that the preservation of a remnant is God's work and the measure of His mercy, not of the remnant's strength. Isaiah makes the remnant the only reason Judah was not Sodom: “Except the LORD of hosts had left unto us a very small remnant, we should have been as Sodom” (Isa 1:9). Paul quotes him to the same end, that of a multitude “a remnant shall be saved” (Rom 9:27). And John sees the church kept alive in a prepared place, where “the woman fled into the wilderness, where she hath a place prepared of God” (Rev 12:6). Elijah was told that seven thousand were left, “all the knees which have not bowed unto Baal” (1Ki 19:18), and he had not known of one.

Usage

"“Even so then at this present time also there is a remnant according to the election of grace” (Rom 11:5) — three valleys held since the thirteenth century."

"“Except the LORD of hosts had left unto us a very small remnant, we should have been as Sodom” (Isa 1:9) — civil rights granted by the Letters Patent of 1848."

"“the woman fled into the wilderness, where she hath a place prepared of God” (Rev 12:6) — the synod and Table seated in the town."
